channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Vietnam launches upgraded National Database on Legal Documents
item.description: VietnamNet: “In the coming time, the database is envisioned as a leading digital legal knowledge platform based on five strategic pillars, including full digitalisation of the legal document lifecycle, an interconnected legal data ecosystem, expanded AI use for legal analysis and alerts, a national big data platform on law, and broader digital legal knowledge for society at large.”

item.title: This Creative Studio Released a “Ciggiedex” of Chinese Cigarette Brands
item.description: RADII: “…spend a few minutes on the site and it clicks: this isn’t really about cigarettes. It’s about documentation, aesthetics, and the growing instinct among young Chinese creators to catalog the overlooked.”

item.title: Launching XOXO Explore
item.description: XOXO: “Named after what we thought would be a throwaway title for a short-lived GitHub repo, allow us to introduce XOXO Explore. Each festival year now has its own index, featuring the complete lineup of every speaker, performer, artist, and project from that year, along with a detailed (and accurate!) schedule with descriptions, dates, times, and venues meticulously imported from our print attendee guide.”

item.title: China’s DeepSeek releases preview of long-awaited V4 model as AI race intensifies
item.description: CNBC: “Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek on Friday released a preview version of its long-awaited V4 large language model, allowing users to test its new capabilities and features.”

item.title: Trump picked a fight with Anthropic. Now the administration is backing off.
item.description: Politico: “Just two months after President Donald Trump declared a government-wide blacklist of the tech startup’s AI software, cybersecurity worries tied to the company’s powerful new Mythos model have both sides searching for a ceasefire, according to six tech lobbyists and policy experts, including two with ties to the White House.”

item.title: deviantART says artists made $23 million on its platform last year, boasts that it was “100% right” to embrace generative AI
item.description: Tubefilter: “Will we see deviantART be a creator economy force alongside YouTube and TikTok in 2026? Thousands of artists are looking for a new home platform after X’s descent into Grokland–but will they be willing to make money on a website that is still doggedly pro-AI?”

item.title: The Iranian women Trump ‘saved’ from execution are simultaneously real and AI-manipulated
item.description: The Verge: “The collage that Trump posted is, at the very least, AI-modified, Mahsa Alimardani, the associate director of the Technology Threats & Opportunities program at WITNESS, told The Verge. But the women themselves are real.”

item.title: Kevin Weil and Bill Peebles exit OpenAI as company continues to shed ‘side quests’
item.description: TechCrunch: “OpenAI is losing two of the architects of its most ambitious moonshots. Kevin Weil, who led the company’s science research initiative, and Bill Peebles, the researcher behind AI video tool Sora, both announced their departures on Friday.”

item.title: US soldier charged with using classified intel to win $400K Polymarket bet on Maduro raid
item.description: Associated Press: “A U.S. special forces soldier involved in the military operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro has been charged with using classified information about the mission to win more than $400,000 in an online betting market, federal officials announced Thursday.”

item.title: Brazil regulator approves deeper probe into Google’s news content use
item.description: Reuters: “Brazil’s antitrust watchdog CADE approved on Thursday a recommendation to deepen ​investigations into the use of journalistic content ‌by Alphabet’s Google, which would assess potential abuse of the company’s dominant market position.”

item.title: Ombudsman column: The Pentagon is trying to silence me
item.description: Stars and Stripes: “No one should be surprised that they’re kicking out the one person charged by Congress with protecting Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence. For nearly a year, Pentagon leadership has placed more and more restrictions on the mainstream media. The New York Times sued and when the Defense/War Department lost in court, instead of following the judge’s ruling Secretary Hegseth and company pivoted, finding another way to restrict journalists. The judge rejected that attempt, too.”

item.title: UK government records relating to Troubles published by National Archives
item.description: Irish Legal News: “This first batch of files includes records offering fresh insights into the conflict’s early stages, including: the Civil Rights Campaign; the Outbreak of Conflict and the deployment of the Army; and the establishment of the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) in 1972 following the suspension of Stormont.”

item.title: New Coaching Database and License System
item.description: Athletics Ireland: “Athletics Ireland is pleased to announce the launch of its new Coaching Database and License System, designed to enhance the support, recognition, and governance of coaching across the organisation. … Under the new system, all coaches who are registered members of Athletics Ireland, hold a Level 2 or Level 3 coaching qualification, and have completed Garda Vetting will be officially recognised as Licensed Coaches.”

item.title: Bluesky set out to fix social media. Now it’s running into familiar problems
item.description: Fast Company: “Once lauded as the heroic anti-X, a more principled and moralistic Twitterverse, Bluesky now appears to be struggling to retain users and build a sustainable, competitive business model. Its identity as an alternative to Twitter drew in waves of oppositional voices, often labeled ‘Resistance Twitter,’ but that positioning may now be its biggest hurdle.”

item.title: BU students react to OpenAI’s Sora shutdown with relief, fear about artist livelihoods
item.description: The Daily Free Press (Boston University): “Although OpenAI did not provide a concrete reason for terminating Sora, it appears the shutdown was largely driven by financial factors, according to The New York Times. OpenAI earned about $13 billion in revenue, but it expects to spend about $100 billion over the next four years. Theo Hanson, a freshman health science major at Boston University with a minor in fine arts, said the shutdown came as a genuine surprise — but a welcome one.”

item.title: Berlin Museum Oversees Digital Resurrection of Hundreds of Paintings Destroyed During World War II
item.description: ARTNews: “Hundreds of paintings lost to the ravages of war—including multiple works by Peter Paul Rubens, Paolo Veronese, Anthony van Dyck, and Caravaggio—will soon be viewable online courtesy of a digitization initiative by Berlin’s Gemäldegalerie.”

item.title: How did thousands of sensitive LAPD files get leaked? City officials seek explanation
item.description: Los Angeles Times: “In the aftermath of a recent data breach that saw hackers make off with a vast trove of confidential police records, Los Angeles leaders have sought an explanation from the city’s top lawyer, whose office was targeted.”

item.title: New undersea cable cutter risks Internet’s backbone
item.description: Ars Technica: “A Chinese ship has tested a new device capable of slicing through submarine data cables thousands of meters beneath the ocean surface. That demonstration may exacerbate security concerns over a spate of suspected sabotage incidents targeting undersea communications and power cables from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.”

item.title: Gen Z Workers Pick Human-Only Output Over AI-Assisted
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Gen Z workers surveyed said they would trust human-only work over AI-assisted output by more than 2-to-1. The findings come from a new survey by the Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup.”

item.title: Researchers: Chatbots are biased and should not be used for political advice
item.description: University of Copenhagen: “AI Popular chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini are not neutral and tend to favor certain political parties when asked who users should vote for. This makes them unsuitable for providing advice in connection with elections, according to researchers from the University of Copenhagen behind a new analysis of political bias in chatbots.”

item.title: How 2 men claimed an absurd record by driving an old 3-wheel car the length of Africa
item.description: Associated Press: “Englishman Ollie Jenks remembers when his friend first pitched the idea to him. ‘It was so ridiculous I couldn’t say no,’ Jenks said. The proposal by his Canadian buddy Seth Scott, a fellow lover of cars and crazy adventures, was for them to drive a decades-old British-made Reliant Robin car from London to the southern tip of Africa — a 14,000-mile (22,500-kilometer) journey through 22 countries — to set a record for the longest trip in a three-wheeled vehicle.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: MIT researchers build the world’s largest collection of Olympiad-level math problems — and open it to everyone
item.description: MIT CSAIL: “MathNet is the largest high-quality dataset of proof-based math problems ever created, and it is not close. Comprising more than 30,000 expert-authored problems and solutions spanning 47 countries, 17 languages, and 143 competitions, it is five times larger than the next biggest dataset of its kind.”

item.title: New online events calendar helps travelers discover what’s happening throughout state
item.description: Big Island Now: “The new feature allows users to browse curated events by island, making it easier to incorporate festivals, cultural experiences and local activities into itineraries. It helps travelers go beyond traditional planning and discover what’s happening during their stay.”

item.title: Ohio Launches Statewide Dashboard to Tackle Chronic Absenteeism
item.description: Governing: “Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine and Department of Education and Workforce Director Stephen Dackin have announced the launch of a statewide Attendance Dashboard in an effort to combat chronic absenteeism in K-12 public schools. Over 25% of Ohio students were chronically absent last year, missing nearly one month of school.” Over 1/4? Holy crap.

item.title: Firefox 150 Is Now Available for Download, This Is What’s New
item.description: 9to5 Linux: “Highlights of Firefox 150 include support for the GTK emoji picker on Linux to let you insert emoji by using the Ctrl+. keyboard shortcut, and the ability to reorganize PDF pages directly in the Firefox PDF viewer, including moving, copying, and deleting pages.”

item.title: Here’s an open-source Google Circle To Search alternative that works offline
item.description: How-To Geek: “Aditya, the developer, has said that his Circle To Search does not require the internet for text recognition, and it can also detect QR codes, and does Smart Scan offline, without requiring uploading these images to Google servers, which is the case with Google’s version.”

item.title: Even Without Internet Access, Prisoners Are Trying to Benefit From A.I.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “…as hype about the technology has infiltrated prison yards and cellblocks, many inmates are eager to try it out. They’re attending workshops and classes to learn about A.I. They ask friends to send printouts of chatbot answers by snail mail. Some inmates even use contraband cellphones to gain access to the technology. The result? A.I.-generated legal documents, essays, business plans and even a bespoke board game or two.”

item.title: A Woman Is Suing MrBeast’s Company For Alleged Sexual Harassment And Verbal Abuse
item.description: Kotaku: “A woman who previously worked at Beast Industries, the company behind MrBeast’s popular YouTube channel, has filed a lawsuit against the YouTuber’s company claiming she was sexually harassed, verbally abused, and fired after returning from maternity leave. The company says it has extensive evidence that ‘unequivocally refutes her claims.'”

item.title: The White House Intervened on Behalf of Accused Sex Trafficker Andrew Tate During a Federal Investigation
item.description: ProPublica: “Federal authorities were chided for seizing electronic devices from Tate and his brother, and told to return them, records and interviews show. Experts said the intervention was highly inappropriate.”

item.title: Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny top Spotify’s first all-time most streamed artists list
item.description: Associated Press: “It’s her, hi! Taylor Swift has topped Spotify’s first ever list of the most streamed artists of all time, published Thursday morning. She’s followed by Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny. That comes as no surprise: In 2025 the artist born Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio was named the streaming giant’s most played artist of the year for a fourth time, dethroning Swift.”

item.title: Got Bugs? U of G Collecting Samples to Catalogue Canada’s Biodiversity
item.description: University of Guelph: “Whether they’re crawling in the dirt or buzzing around a park, researchers at the University of Guelph want your bugs. It’s part of BugQuest, a nationwide community science project run by the Centre for Biodiversity Genomics (CBG). The goal? To set up 1,000 traps across Canada to survey insect diversity.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: UA data science students launch sports analytics application Hog Charts
item.description: The Arkansas Traveler: “Brady Brown and Wyatt Thompson, two University of Arkansas sophomore data science majors, created Hog Charts, a sports data analytics application they have developed over several months while sharing predictions on their Instagram, @hogcharts.”

item.title: Carnegie Hall Celebrates 15 Years of Making Music at Sing Sing Correctional Facility with Sing Sing Voices, A New Collection of Video Playlists Showcasing Original Songs by Program Participants
item.description: Carnegie Hall: “Carnegie Hall celebrates 15 years of its Musical Connections program this season with Sing Sing Voices, a new collection of video playlists featuring original music created by participants and alumni of the Hall’s long-standing residency at Sing Sing Correctional Facility. Now available to the”

item.title: Deezer says 44% of songs uploaded to its platform daily are AI-generated
item.description: TechCrunch: “Deezer announced on Monday that AI-generated tracks now represent 44% of all new music uploaded to its platform. The company said it’s receiving almost 75,000 AI-generated tracks per day and more than two million per month. The consumption of AI-generated music on the platform is still very low, at 1-3% of total streams, and 85% of these streams are detected as fraudulent and demonetized by the company.”

item.title: Virginia voter support for new data centers collapses from 69% in 2023 to 35% in new poll — Multi-gigawatt, 37-building Digital Gateway project abandoned
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Just 35% of Virginia voters now say they would be comfortable with a new data center going up in their community, down from 69% in 2023, according to a Washington Post-Schar School poll published Wednesday.”

item.title: Meta to track workers’ clicks and keystrokes to train AI
item.description: BBC: “Meta will start tracking the way employees work, including their keystrokes and mouse clicks, to train its artificial intelligence (AI) models. The company, which owns Instagram and Facebook, told workers on Tuesday that a new tool will run on Meta’s computers and internal apps, logging their activity to be used as training data for AI technology.”

item.title: Apple and Google are reportedly pointing users to ‘nudify’ apps
item.description: Engadget: “Earlier this year it was revealed that Apple and Google were offering ‘nudify’ apps on their stores despite having clear policies barring such content. Nearly three months later, such apps are not only still available, but being actively promoted on the iOS App Store and Google Play, according to a new report from the Tech Transparency Project (TTP).”

item.title: Los Angeles becomes the first major school district to require screen time limits
item.description: NBC News: “The Los Angeles Unified School District’s board voted Tuesday to restrict students’ use of laptops and tablets in class and encourage pen-and-paper assignments instead, making it the first major American school system to do so.”

item.title: Police pull the plug on mobile billboard targeting Janet Mills on data centers
item.description: Sun Journal: “Hallowell police on Thursday pulled the plug on efforts to enlighten Gov. Janet Mills about the dangers of data centers. Police Chief Christopher Giles said officers cited the driver of a mobile, electronic billboard urging Mills to sign a bill that would institute a moratorium on data centers.”

item.title: The AI Slop Loop
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Last year, after spending a few days at a work summit in Austria, I asked Perplexity for the latest news related to SEO and AI search. It responded with details about a supposed ‘September 2025 “Perspective” Core Algorithm Update’ that Google had just rolled out, emphasizing ‘deeper expertise’ and ‘completion of the user journey.’ It sounded plausible enough �� if you don’t live and breathe Google core updates. Unfortunately for Perplexity, I do.”

item.title: More time spent on social media is linked to a thinner cerebral cortex in young adolescents
item.description: PsyPost: “New research published in the journal NeuroImage suggests that spending more time on social media is associated with physical differences in the developing brains of young adolescents. Specifically, children who spent more hours on digital platforms exhibited a thinner outer layer of the brain in areas responsible for attention, memory, and emotional control.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: New website helps landowners track wildfire recovery, view history
item.description: University of Nebraska-Lincoln: “Following historic wildfires that have burned nearly one million acres of Nebraska grazing lands this spring, the University of Nebraska–Lincoln has launched a new online hub that integrates science, mapping and field-based documentation in one place.”

item.title: New cannabis database aims to boost safety & transparency for Nevada consumers on 4/20
item.description: KTNV: “The agency has launched the Metrc Item Catalog, a database that tracks nearly 50,000 products sold at licensed dispensaries across Nevada. The system allows users to view key details like lab test results, ingredients, potency, and whether a product has been flagged or placed on hold.”

item.title: Enthusiasts build an interactive online ‘Listening Museum’ of iconic mechanical keyboard audio samples — 36 mechanical masterpieces available for you to audibly try out
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “This is a collection of 36 iconic to modern classic keyboards that have been multisampled and put into an interactive site. Just click on any of the keyboards represented on the page, turn up your speakers, and bash away.”

item.title: Book bans and attempted bans remain at record highs, with ‘Sold’ topping the list
item.description: Associated Press: “Book bans and attempted bans remain at record highs, according to the American Library Association. And efforts to have titles removed have never been more coordinated or politicized.”

item.title: YouTube expands its AI likeness detection technology to celebrities
item.description: TechCrunch: “YouTube is expanding its new ‘likeness detection’ technology, which identifies AI-generated content, such as deepfakes, to people within the entertainment industry, the company announced on Tuesday.”

item.title: Bing is the anti-AI search engine you should be using
item.description: PC World: “Searching via AI doesn’t just hurt content creators–it also mashes up what you’re looking for in a tasteless glob of names and numbers. If you’re searching for recommendations, start with a search engine that improves the experience. No, not Google. Microsoft Bing.”

item.title: Some Unknown Group Is Reportedly Using Claude Mythos Without Permission
item.description: Gizmodo: “In a very cagily-written story from Bloomberg, Anthropic confirmed Tuesday that it has received a report that an unauthorized mystery group is accessing Claude Mythos—the model it says is too dangerous to release.”

item.title: EU imposes sanctions, blacklists Euromore and Pravfond for spreading Kremlin disinformation
item.description: Mezha: “According to the official website of the Council of the European Union, the sanctions list includes the media platform Euromore, which is part of a pro-Kremlin information network. The European Union assesses that Euromore spreads and amplifies Russian narratives, tailoring them for a European audience, and also disseminates content that questions the legitimacy of EU institutions and justifies Russia’s war against Ukraine.”

item.title: Authors Guild Addresses Publishers’ AI Use
item.description: Publishers Weekly: “The Authors Guild has released a statement criticizing publishing professionals’ use of AI tools following a report first published in the Bookseller that some editors have been uploading authors’ personal information, including manuscripts, into consumer-facing LLMs like ChatGPT.”

item.title: Online gaming might contribute to creativity, study finds
item.description: PsyPost: “A study in Taiwan found that individuals who were more motivated to play online games tended to show higher post-game imagination. Imagination, in turn, was associated with greater creativity, indicating that gaming motivation might contribute to creativity.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court Records and Briefs: The Arguments That Shaped America, Now Freely Available
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “Thanks to a generous gift of materials from the Wolf Law Library at the William & Mary Law School, and the Internet Archive’s mission to digitize and provide universal access to knowledge, we are pleased to share more than 125,000 U.S. Supreme Court records and briefs.”

item.title: Relive the PC magazine cover disk era with 758-strong archive.org CD-ROM collection — 1.2TB treasure trove also includes Floppy Disks from as early as 1993
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Earlier today, our sister site PC Gamer revealed that there is now a treasure trove of its cover disks (floppies, CDs, and DVDs) archived and ready to enjoy. PC Gamer’s headline highlights the 758 cover disks on the Internet Archive, but there are actually even more gems to be found. Our search uncovered over 1,500 PC Gamer software archives, thanks to a trove of floppy disk offerings from yesteryear.”

item.title: Gates Foundation reviewing Jeffrey Epstein ties, will slash 20% of staff, WSJ reports
item.description: CNBC: “The Gates Foundation has launched an external review of the philanthropy’s past ties with notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. To cut costs, the Gates Foundation will eliminate up to 500 jobs, or about 20% of its staff, by 2030, the Journal reported, citing an email to staff that the newspaper reviewed announcing both the job cuts and Epstein ties review.”

item.title: Character.AI users can now role-play classic books like ‘Pride and Prejudice’
item.description: Mashable: “The artificial intelligence entertainment platform Character.AI introduced on Thursday a feature allowing users to role-play in more than 20 classic books, including Hamlet, Alice in Wonderland, Pride and Prejudice, The Great Gatsby.”

item.title: Who is Emily Hart? How an Indian medical student fooled ‘dumb’ MAGA fans with AI
item.description: Business Today: “Meet “Emily Hart.” To her millions of fans, she was a gun-loving, beer-drinking nurse who looked like Jennifer Lawrence and loved ‘Christ is King.’ But in reality, she was the creation of ‘Sam,’ a 22-year-old orthopaedic surgeon in training in India. According to a Wired report, Sam (name changed) used Google’s AI tools to create a fake conservative influencer to pay his medical school bills. He created a digital fantasy that the American right couldn’t stop clicking on.”

item.title: Former Republican Rep. Devin Nunes out as Trump Media CEO
item.description: Politico: “The C-suite overhaul lands after years of repeated losses at Trump Media, a company that was once billed as a conservative challenger to Silicon Valley giants and the next gem in Trump’s vast business empire. The company recorded a net loss of more than $712 million and revenues of $3.7 million in 2025.”

item.title: Meta has misled users about scam ads on Facebook and Instagram, lawsuit says
item.description: Engadget: “The lawsuit, which was first reported by Wired, alleges that Meta has run afoul of consumer protection laws in Washington D.C. for misleading Facebook and Instagram users about scams on its apps and that the company has ‘chased profits rather than protecting its users.’ The filing includes numerous examples of alleged scam ads that CFA says it found in Meta’s ad library.”

item.title: Most serious cyberattacks against the UK now from Russia, Iran and China, cyber chief will say
item.description: Associated Press: “The most serious cyberattacks in the U.K. are now carried out by hostile nations including Russia, Iran and China, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) will say in a speech Wednesday.”

item.title: Sam Altman’s Creepy Eyeball-Scanning Company Gets in Bed With Zoom and Tinder
item.description: Gizmodo: “On Friday, both Tinder and Zoom announced partnerships with Altman’s World, the company behind the creepy, eyeball-scanning orb that is meant to prove users are human.”

item.title: New Study Could Show How TikTok’s Algorithm Affects Youth Mental Health
item.description: Georgia Tech: “A Georgia Tech-led research team is conducting a multi-year study using data from more than 10,000 adolescents to investigate how TikTok’s recommendation algorithm and passive content consumption impact youth mental health.”

item.title: Dozens of AI disease-prediction models were trained on dubious data
item.description: Nature: “Dubious data sets are being used to train artificial-intelligence models that are designed to predict people’s risk of stroke and diabetes, researchers report in a preprint1 on medRxiv. Some of the models seem to have been used in clinical settings, although it’s not clear whether this has led to flawed diagnoses. At least two journals are investigating studies that used these data sets.”

item.title: Tiny cameras in earbuds let users talk with AI about what they see
item.description: University of Washington: “The prototype system called VueBuds takes low-resolution, black-and-white images, which it transmits over Bluetooth to a phone or other nearby device. A small artificial intelligence model on the device then answers questions about the images within around a second. For privacy, all of the processing happens on the device, a small light turns on when the system is recording, and users can immediately delete images.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Taliban Launch New Website to Share Information on Their Activities
item.description: Kabul Now: “The Taliban have announced that they have launched a new website named ‘Permukhtag’ to provide information about the activities of the group. The website was inaugurated today (Sunday, April 19) in the presence of Taliban officials at the Arg.”

item.title: Minecraft is bringing life-sized biomes to TwitchCon Rotterdam–plus a Tubbo competition, community hangout, and more
item.description: Tubefilter: “Minecraft is headed to TwitchCon. The iconic sandbox video game will have a serious spotlight at this year’s TwitchCon Rotterdam, running May 30-31 at the Rotterdam Ahoy complex in the Netherlands.”

item.title: National Archives of India digitises 20 crore pages—nearly 60% completed in 2 years
item.description: The Print: “The National Archives of India has digitised nearly 60 per cent of the archival records. Union Culture Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat announced on Monday that this is a landmark step in preserving Bharat’s documentary heritage. Out of the 34 crore pages of precious archival material, the National Archives of India (NAI) has digitised more than 20 crore pages.”

item.title: Trinity Christian College to transfer majority of archives to Michigan university before spring closure
item.description: Chicago Tribune: “After the board of trustees voted to shutter the college Nov. 3, the future of Trinity’s records as well as the Van Namen Dutch Heritage Center housed there largely remained a mystery to the general public. [Kyle] McCarrell said about half of the archive’s materials were well-organized ahead of the impending closure announcement, but categorizing what remains has been largely left up to him.”

item.title: Indie Animation Is Having a Moment on YouTube
item.description: Gizmodo: “A recent report from the company’s Trends and Culture team dug into the indie boom for shows like Amazing Digital Circus (whose final episode hits theaters in June) and Helluva Boss. A survey conducted in April 2025 shows 61% of animation fans between the ages of 14 and 24 are more into works from indie creators rather than ones from a major studio.”

item.title: See Photos from Archives of Nine Photographers Going to Center for Creative Photography
item.description: ARTNews: “The Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona in Tucson has acquired the archives of nine photographers: Laura Aguilar, Jack Dykinga, Jody Forster, Frank Gohlke, Mark Klett, Nathan Lyons, Stephen Marc, Patrick Nagatani, and Susan Wood.”

item.title: Advertisers are gearing up to hit Google with mass arbitration claims worth billions
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google’s legal troubles over its search and ad tech businesses are entering a new phase — one that could expose the company to billions in payouts from advertisers seeking damages after U.S. courts found it illegally monopolized key digital ad markets.”

item.title: Testing OCR with Chrome Built-in AI
item.description: Raymond Camden: “I had a great question in my session on Chrome’s Built-in AI which led to a bit of investigating last night. The question involved how well Chrome’s AI could do OCR on an image. I had a demo in my presentation showing using AI to describe an image and another to generate a list of tags, but not one specifically for OCR. Here’s what I found.”

item.title: Meet the D.C. devotees of a very niche arcade game
item.description: The 51st: “Killer Queen is a 10-player arcade game designed to get you off of your phone and playing with strangers. In one D.C. bar, dedicated fans are trying to get new players hooked.”

item.title: The Onion Says It Has a Deal to Take Over Alex Jones’ Infowars, Plans to Relaunch Right-Wing Site as Parody of Itself
item.description: Variety: “Satire site the Onion says that it has — after 17 months legal wrangling — successfully landed a deal allowing it take over Infowars, the right-wing conspiracy-fueled site run by Alex Jones.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: DLARC Adds New Radio Resources to Celebrate World Amateur Radio Day
item.description: Internet Archive Blog: “Internet Archive’s Digital Library of Amateur Radio & Communications, a library devoted to ham radio, shortwave, and related topics, announces a number of new collections to mark World Amateur Radio Day.”

item.title: New Smithsonian Online Exhibition Celebrates the Art and Skill of Traditional Trades
item.description: Smithsonian: “The Smithsonian’s Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage today launched ‘Built by Hand: Skilled Artisans in the Traditional Trades,’ a new online exhibition that highlights the creativity, knowledge and experiences of skilled artisans and building trades. The exhibition features in depth profiles of stone masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, stained glass artists and other skilled tradespeople whose work helps shape and preserve the nation’s built environment.”

item.title: I stopped using LM Studio once I found this open-source alternative
item.description: MakeUseOf: “The alternative that eventually ended up replacing LM Studio for me is Jan. It’s a desktop application that lets you run LLMs fully offline — much like LM Studio, but not only is it completely free, it’s also open-source, with all the source code being available on GitHub. There are no licensing surprises, no proprietary lock-ins, and no fine print you need to worry about.”

item.title: Voting is live: Help choose the next Doodle for Google winner
item.description: Google Blog: “Today, we’re thrilled to share that our judges have selected five finalists from the tens of thousands of amazing submissions we received from across the country. … Read on to meet our judges, check out the amazing finalist Doodles, and learn how you can vote for the national winner.”

item.title: Google denies involvement in $125 million Chromebook graft case in Indonesia
item.description: Associated Press: “Google’s investment in Indonesia’s ride-hailing company GoTo wasn’t in anyway connected to the country’s Education Ministry’s decision to procure Chromebooks for schools during COVID-19 pandemic, former Google executives testified in court on Monday.”

item.title: Should you really trust health advice from an AI chatbot?
item.description: BBC: “It is hard to know how many people like Abi are using chatbots for health advice. The technology has ballooned in popularity and even if you’re not actively seeking advice from artificial intelligence, you’ll be served it up at the top of an internet search. The quality of the advice being given out by artificial intelligence is concerning England’s top doctor.”

item.title: Thinking about AI can make people more critical of human decision-makers, study shows
item.description: University of Exeter: “AI may influence public attitudes by making people more aware of the limitations of human decision-making, a new study shows. New research suggests when citizens are prompted to think about AI decision-making, they subsequently judge human decision-makers more critically.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Ngā Tapuwae Trails content to be preserved in NZ’s national digital archive
item.description: New Zealand Ministry for Culture & Heritage: “Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage confirms it will preserve its website ‘Ngā Tapuwae Trails’, which presents First World War trails and location-based stories, after Anzac Day.”

item.title: the Reddit announcement
item.description: Spotted on Reddit: Insights64, a search engine for chess positions. From “I’ve been toying with this idea for a while and finally came around to it! Its a tool that let’s you find positions in real games (from Lichess only for now) based on specific pieces in the board or specific positional patterns.”

item.title: News organizations reconsider ties to AI company Nota after plagiarism findings
item.description: Poynter: “In the week after Poynter published its investigation into extensive plagiarism found on a network of local news sites, the artificial intelligence company behind those sites lost a major client and fired the remaining contractor on the project.”

item.title: Markdown.new + bookmarklet
item.description: Information Overload: “Markdown.new is a nice little tool to convert a webpage into Markdown without any fuss. To make it even easier, I created a bookmarklet to instantly convert the page you’re viewing to Markdown.”

item.title: Nobody talks about this polished open-source note-taking app, and I don’t get it
item.description: MakeUseOf: “With note-taking apps, I’ve tried far more than I’m willing to admit. A few, like Obsidian, Notion, and even OneNote, have been solid. However, no matter the tool I try, I’ve always come back to Joplin.”

item.title: VC is being rewired by AI
item.description: VC Cafe: “While venture capital remains a relationship-driven business at its core, the industry is rapidly transitioning and adopting AI automation across the various tasks of a VC fund.”

item.title: I grew up on Zoom and social media. Protect Illinois kids, teens from the dangers of AI
item.description: Chicago Sun-Times: “It’s reasonable to ask our representatives to pass a bill that requires the most powerful AI companies to be honest about what they know, protect the kids using their products and let someone check their safety work. For a generation that grew up as the test subjects of the ‘move fast and figure it out later’ approach, it might be one of the most reasonable things our legislators can do.”

item.title: Guest comment: Your nonprofit needs an AI policy—now
item.description: Reno News & Review: “Leaner nonprofits have a lot of reasons to leverage AI. Grant-writing and volunteer coordination are two areas in which I can see AI being quite helpful. The question isn’t about whether an organization is going to use AI; it’s about whether it does it with integrity and purpose. Set a policy now.”

item.title: Crazed World of Warcraft gamer plays game with 3D-printed hot dog controller — the left wiener quad-array controls movement, the right triggers abilities
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “Specifically, addison2k conceptualized and built a hot dog-based game controller. This smoky-flavored, tactile, dead-flesh device features a pair of quad-array hot dog silos. As designed, the left weiner quartet controls movement, and the right triggers abilities.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Duolingo stops evaluating workers based on how much AI they use
item.description: TechSpot: “In a classic example of a CEO admitting he got too carried away on the AI hype train, Duolingo boss Luis von Ahn has confirmed the company will no longer assess employees’ performance based on how much they use AI for work tasks.”

item.title: Under fire for AI image, John Waldron to resign from House seat
item.description: Oklahoma Voice: “A state representative under scrutiny for sending an inappropriate AI-generated image to a woman will resign Oct. 1 from the state House. Rep. John Waldron, D-Tulsa, submitted a resignation letter Thursday to the Governor’s Office, which shared the document with Oklahoma Voice.”

item.title: Out of 11 million photos, one news photo taken in the heart of Sydney is nagging Harry
item.description: Sydney Morning Herald: “In a secret climate-controlled facility in Sydney’s west, photo specialist Harry Hollinsworth is working through The Sydney Morning Herald’s archives to save photos that brought history to life. The Herald celebrates its 195th birthday on Saturday, April 18 and Hollinsworth is part of a five-year digitisation project that is creating a single online archive of Nine Entertainment’s media companies to mark the Herald’s bicentenary in 2031.”

item.title: ‘Like handing out the blueprint to a bank vault’: Why AI led one company to abandon open source
item.description: ZDNet: “Cal is moving its flagship open-source program to a proprietary model because it can’t cope with the dangers of AI hacking its open code.”

item.title: Alleged FSU shooter consulted ChatGPT on when to attack, sexual scenarios with a minor
item.description: Orlando Weekly: “Other conversations detail graphic sexual descriptions of a minor and another college student, sexual conversations about family members, and repeated references to Timothy McVeigh, the Oklahoma City bomber. He also consulted the chatbot about weapons, how Florida treats school shooters and the busiest time at the student union — where prosecutors allege he murdered two and wounded five others just before noon last April. They’re seeking the death penalty.”

item.title: How the rewards app Freecash scammed its way to the top of the app stores
item.description: TechCrunch: “The app has been marketed as a way to make money just by scrolling TikTok — and jumped to the top of the app stores in recent months, peaking at the No. 2 position in the U.S. App Store. In truth, Freecash pays users to play mobile games — all the while collecting a heaping amount of sensitive data, according to cybersecurity company Malwarebytes.”

item.title: Not all networks can handle AI traffic – and experts are sounding alarms
item.description: The Register: “AI is reshaping the demands on network infrastructure, and many organizations are not prepared – including some of the so-called neocloud providers offering AI services. A study by analyst biz Omdia finds that many rent-a-GPU providers have scaled up their compute infrastructure to handle AI workloads, but their networking infrastructure is becoming a critical constraint.”

item.title: We Don’t Really Know How A.I. Works. That’s a Problem.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “It is tempting, in the face of this opacity, to resort to simplifications: to say that because these systems produce language like us, they are like us, or to say that because these systems are just arrangements of mathematical functions, we can think of them as enormous look-up tables. But both of these claims are too dismissive — neither can adequately explain the superhuman abilities and strangely ingenuous behavior of A.I. models.”

item.title: Martha Cooper photographed graffiti’s origins. Decades later, she’s still at it.
item.description: Gothamist: “Cooper had grown up in her father’s camera shop in Baltimore and spent much of her time looking at the world through the other side of a lens. Where others saw vandalism that needed to be scrubbed away, she saw energy and beauty. She befriended a young graffiti writer named Edwin Serrano, known as He3, who brought her into the underground, thus launching a remarkable career documenting street art that’s spanned six decades — and is still going.” Good morning, Internet…
